extraction.segment_function: Analyzing the Greek and Latin etymology of action, the historical shift from interdependence to ruler-subject relations, and the inherent boundlessness, unpredictability, and relationship-establishing capacity of human action that makes human affairs frail.

claims.claim: Greek and Latin languages contain two interrelated words for the verb 'to act', reflecting an original division between the initial beginning made by a single person and the subsequent achievement carried out by many.
claims.supporting_excerpt: In order to illustrate what is at stake here we may remember that Greek and Latin, unlike the modern languages, contain two altogether different and yet interrelated words with which to designate the verb “to act.”

claims.claim: Action inherently possesses a boundless quality because every reaction acts as a new independent action that triggers chain reactions, meaning even the smallest act in limited circumstances can change every constellation.
claims.supporting_excerpt: These consequences are boundless, because action, though it may proceed from nowhere, so to speak, acts into a medium where every reaction becomes a chain reaction and where every process is the cause of new processes.
qualifications: applies regardless of the specific content of action

definitions.definition: An activity performed among and in relation to other acting beings where the actor is simultaneously a doer and a sufferer, characterized by boundless consequences, chain reactions, and the establishment of relationships.

distinctions.distinction: The former originally designated the beginning, leading, or setting into motion of an enterprise by a single person, whereas the latter originally designated the achievement, bearing, and finishing of the enterprise in which many join.

must_not_be_lost: The historical shift from primus inter pares leadership to isolated ruler-subject dynamics.
The connection between the human condition of natality and the inherent frailty of human institutions and laws.
Moderation as a primary political virtue and hubris as the political temptation par excellence.
